For an old proper trace with unit continuous normal, integrating parallel section measures gives the two-sided threshold expansion with coefficient equal to its proper section area. The upper continuity bound follows from compactness and projection into the old section plane. Convex interpolation with an interior point on the required side gives the matching lower limit. In dimension one proper coarea is one. Strictly full or empty traces have a positive gap and contribute zero threshold coefficient.

Uniformity of the actual shell loss over bounded threshold speeds follows from the nullity of the old cutting plane for every source cone law. Off that plane all radial points and bounded threshold speeds eventually give the same indicator. The shell factor then supplies the uniform first-order coefficient L_j.

One positive proper section per cap persists in a fixed height neighborhood for small deformation because old interior points on both sides remain interior under the contraction. Thus the deformed tail is continuous and strictly decreasing there. Bracketing by speeds on both sides of -(L_j+q)/S_j gives the claimed inverse expansion uniformly for bounded q.

The weighted sum of inverse displacements is continuous and strictly decreasing in common mass. The leading term is minus epsilon times the positive scalar sum(rho_j/S_j) times q-q_c. This brackets a unique nearby common mass and proves the stated derivative. Positive circuit weights with unchanged weighted threshold budget leave the assigned-plane weighted margin unchanged, so the shifted caps cover each such plane.

The strict shared-source condition bounds the exact raw derivative by a number below beta M'(0+). Thus the common normalized budget is strictly below beta on every selected circuit, for the same deformation and sufficiently small epsilon. Finite old slack covers remain slack by the nested measured fibers and continuous total mass.

If a null base were in the convex hull of the positive-volume bases, represent it by a finite convex combination and choose one source with positive coefficient. Fix points in the other fibers and vary the point in that positive source. Convexity then places a translated positive multiple of the source body in the null fiber, a contradiction.

The finite positive-base hull is compact and nonempty. A strict separation from the null base gives a pure-base closed cap through that null base with zero measured mass. This remains valid when the positive-base hull has lower affine dimension. An old interior point of a positive-volume fiber has positive depth from its own inball, so beta>0 and the new null points lie strictly below the old normalized budget. The finite measured cover bounds all other points as before.
